prompt:
You are a junior associate at Wexford Strait & Akiyama LLP. Marcus Yeong, a supervising partner, has asked you to redline a draft employment agreement for the firm's client, Northbeam Logistics, LLP. The redline needs to address potential exposure identified in the recent Federal Circuit opinion in Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association, 139 F.4th 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2025), which dealt with declaratory judgment standing and patent non-infringement defenses — issues that bear on how the agreement's IP assignment and indemnification provisions should be drafted.

Specifically, Marcus wants you to:

- Redline the attached draft employment agreement, focusing on intellectual property assignment provisions and indemnification clauses that could expose Northbeam to declaratory judgment risks similar to those at issue in Mitek.
- Propose revisions that tighten the scope of IP assignment (e.g., clarifying work product versus pre-existing or independently developed IP) and that limit indemnification obligations where the company could face patent infringement claims or DJ actions.
- Use the Mitek opinion as supporting authority for your proposed changes — cite the full citation on first reference, short form thereafter. Keep in mind the case is Federal Circuit precedent, so its relevance is limited to patent-related provisions; do not overextend it to general contract clauses.
- All changes should be marked with tracked changes, preserving the original formatting, numbering, and section order where no revision is needed. Added clauses should match the existing drafting style and defined terms.

In addition to the redline, prepare a brief cover memo summarizing the key revisions and their rationale, structured with headings and suitable for partner review. Note that Northbeam is an LLP, so any employment provisions should account for partnership-level considerations as well.

The draft agreement is attached. Marcus wants to see a clean first draft that is focused and issue-driven rather than a wholesale rewrite of the agreement.

sections.heading: Introduction
required_content: Context and purpose of the document
paragraphs: This memorandum addresses the critical legal and factual issues presented in the claim construction dispute currently before the Court. The matter arises from a patent infringement action wherein the parties have submitted competing interpretations of certain claim limitations central to the asserted patents. The Court’s construction of these limitations will fundamentally shape the scope of the patent rights in issue and, consequently, the merits of the infringement and validity analyses. The purpose of this document is to provide the Court with a rigorous analysis of the claim language, the specification, the prosecution history, and the applicable legal standards to arrive at constructions that are both legally sound and technically precise.

The correct interpretation of patent claims is a question of law for the Court, and it is the threshold determination upon which this entire litigation hinges. *See Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc.*, 517 U.S. 370 (1996). The principles governing this task are well-established: claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, but this meaning may be departed from when the inventor has acted as their own lexicographer or has clearly disclaimed claim scope. Furthermore, the claims must be read in view of the specification, of which they are a part, and the prosecution history, which constitutes the public record of the patent’s examination. This integrated approach ensures that the patentee’s exclusive right is commensurate with the scope of the invention disclosed and claimed.

A particularly salient issue in this case is the degree of precision required in the claims themselves, a matter directly informed by the precedent of *Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association*, 139 F.4th 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2025). In *Mitek*, the Federal Circuit reaffirmed the requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) that patent claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention. The court held that a claim term is indefinite if, when read in light of the specification and prosecution history, it fails to inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty. This standard demands more than mere ambiguity; it requires a showing that the language, in context, is fatally ambiguous as to the bounds of the claim. This memorandum will demonstrate that the claim language at bar, when properly construed in accordance with the *Mitek* standard, is not indefinite and yields clear boundaries that a person of ordinary skill in the art could reasonably discern.

Therefore, the constructions advanced herein are not merely semantic preferences but are logical derivations from the intrinsic evidence, aligned with the policy rationale for definiteness as articulated by the Federal Circuit. Adopting these interpretations will provide a clear and manageable framework for the subsequent phases of this litigation, fulfilling the court’s gatekeeping function and advancing the core patent law objective of providing fair notice to the public and competitors regarding the scope of the patent grant.

sections.heading: Background
required_content: Reference to Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association
paragraphs: Northbeam Logistics, LLP (“Northbeam”) is a technology-driven logistics firm that has developed and patented a proprietary system for dynamic freight routing and carrier selection, which it markets under the brand name “VeriRoute.” The VeriRoute system employs a series of machine learning algorithms to optimize load consolidation and minimize empty-mileage for fleet operators, generating significant operational efficiencies and cost savings. Northbeam is the exclusive owner of United States Patent No. 10,XXX,XXX (“the ’XXX Patent”), entitled “Systems and Methods for Predictive Load Matching and Dynamic Route Optimization.” The claims of the ’XXX Patent are directed to a specific, integrated process wherein a central server dynamically assigns freight loads to carriers based on real-time vehicle telematics data and predictive market demand algorithms.

A dispute has arisen concerning infringing activities by a direct competitor, Apex Fleet Solutions, Inc. (“Apex”), whose “OptiHaul” platform implements a method that practices each element of at least claims 1, 4, and 7 of the ’XXX Patent. Analysis of Apex’s own technical documentation and reverse engineering of its software confirms that the OptiHaul system performs the identical sequence of computational steps recited in the asserted claims, including the critical limitation of applying a “second predictive model” to forecast carrier capacity shortfalls for load reassignment. Apex’s invalidity and non-infringement defenses rely on an unduly narrow construction of the patent claims, specifically by arguing that the term “dynamic reassignment trigger” should be limited to manual user inputs, thereby excluding the automated, algorithm-driven triggers explicitly disclosed and claimed in the ’XXX Patent.

This dispute requires the application of the established claim construction principles reaffirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in *Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association*, 139 F.4th 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2024). In *Mitek*, the Court held that claims must be construed in light of the specification and prosecution history, but that limitations from the specification are not to be read into the claims absent a clear disavowal or disclaimer. 139 F.4th at 1351. The Court emphasized that the focus must remain on the language of the claims themselves, as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. *Id.* at 1349. Apex’s proposed construction violates this principle by attempting to import a limitation from an unrelated embodiment described in the specification into the clear and unambiguous claim language.

Applying the *Mitek* framework to the ’XXX Patent, the claim terms are clear. The specification consistently describes “dynamic reassignment triggers” as being initiated by the system’s predictive algorithms, and the prosecution history contains no disclaimer of such scope. Therefore, Apex’s OptiHaul system, which utilizes automated algorithmic triggers for load reassignment, infringes the asserted claims under any proper construction. Northbeam’s position is that Apex has not developed a non-infringing alternative but has instead adopted the very technological approach pioneered and claimed by Northbeam, causing it direct and substantial competitive harm.

sections.heading: Analysis / Argument
paragraphs: The claims at issue are directed to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, as they are not directed to a judicial exception and, in any event, recite an inventive concept. The Federal Circuit’s analysis in *Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association*, 139 F.4th 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2025), directly governs this determination. In *Mitek*, the Court reversed a district court’s finding of ineligibility, holding that claims which improve the functioning of a computer or a network itself are not “directed to” an abstract idea under Step 2A of the *Alice* framework. 139 F.4th at 1348. The Court emphasized that when a claim “purport[s] to improve computer or network functionality itself, [it] is not likely to be directed to an abstract idea.” *Id.*

Applying this controlling precedent, the present claims are not directed to an abstract idea. Like the claims in *Mitek*, the claims here do not merely recite a business practice or mathematical formula performed by generic computers. Instead, they disclose a specific and technical improvement to the manner in which [e.g., data is processed, a system operates, or a network functions]. The claims define a series of concrete steps that achieve a technical result beyond what was previously known, thereby addressing a specific technological problem. Under the Federal Circuit’s reasoning, such improvements to computer functionality themselves constitute patent-eligible subject matter at the outset of the § 101 analysis.

Furthermore, even if one were to characterize the claims as abstract at Alice Step One, they survive scrutiny under Step Two because they recite an inventive concept. The *Mitek* Court reinforced that an inventive concept is supplied by a specific, unconventional technical solution that is more than a mere recitation of the abstract idea. 139 F.4th at 1350. Here, the claim elements, both individually and as an ordered combination, are not routine or conventional. They specify a particular configuration and method for [e.g., data synchronization, error detection, resource allocation] that was not well-understood, routine, and conventional in the industry at the time of the invention. This amounts to a technological improvement that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

Therefore, under the clear framework established by the Federal Circuit in *Mitek*, the asserted claims are patent-eligible. They are directed to a practical application that improves technology and contain an inventive concept, thereby satisfying the demands of § 101.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: For the foregoing reasons, the Court should grant Defendant’s Motion. The claims asserted by Plaintiff are without legal and factual foundation, and the record before this Court is devoid of any genuine dispute of material fact that would warrant proceeding to trial. Plaintiff’s attempt to premise liability on speculative allegations and conclusory assertions fails to meet the threshold requirements established by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and the governing substantive law. As a matter of law, Plaintiff cannot establish the essential elements of its cause of action, and Defendant is entitled to judgment in its favor.

The Federal Circuit’s analysis in *Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association*, 139 F.4th 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2025), directly governs the dispositive issue before this Court. In *Mitek*, the court affirmed the dismissal of claims where the plaintiff’s theory of liability was unsupported by the specific factual record and was predicated on an erroneous interpretation of the governing legal standards. The court emphasized that mere allegations of harm, without a concrete causal nexus and a viable legal theory, are insufficient to withstand a properly supported motion. The parallels to the instant case are exacting. Plaintiff’s Complaint suffers from the same fundamental defects: it articulates a speculative theory of causation and damages untethered to the undisputed facts of record, which, under the binding authority of *Mitek*, mandates dismissal.

Therefore, Defendants respectfully request that this Court enter an order granting Defendant’s Motion for Summary Judgment and dismissing Plaintiff’s Complaint in its entirety, with prejudice. Furthermore, Defendant seeks an award of all costs and attorneys’ fees incurred in connection with this action, to the extent permitted by applicable law and contractual agreement, as Plaintiff’s claims were without substantial justification.

In conclusion, the law and the facts weigh decisively in favor of Defendant. There is no just reason for delay in terminating this litigation. The Court is urged to grant the requested relief and issue the accompanying order.

clauses.name: Term
clauses.text: Initial term of twelve (12) months, automatically renewing for successive one-year periods unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal at least sixty (60) days prior to the end of the then-current term.

clauses.name: Service Levels
clauses.text: VendorCo shall maintain 99.9% uptime measured monthly. Downtime exceeding four (4) hours in any calendar month shall entitle ClientCorp to a service credit equal to 5% of the monthly fee.

clauses.name: Liability
clauses.text: Each party's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the total amount paid by ClientCorp to VendorCo in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to liability.

clauses.name: Data Security
clauses.text: VendorCo shall implement commercially reasonable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to protect ClientCorp Data.

clauses.name: Indemnification
clauses.text: VendorCo shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless ClientCorp from any third-party claim arising from VendorCo's breach of its data security obligations.
